```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Bae_2019_vancomycin"))$reference`
* Description: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Bae_2019_vancomycin"))$description`
* Article: [Pharmaceutics 2019;11(5):224](https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics11050224)
  (open access, PMC6572512)

Bae et al. built this model as the population prior of an open-source
R Shiny Bayesian therapeutic-drug-monitoring tool for Korean patients,
arguing that the Western-population priors in commercial TDM software
over-predict vancomycin concentrations in Korean patients and cannot
represent hemodialysis or continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT).

# Population

Routine TDM data from 220 adult inpatients (1020 vancomycin
concentrations) treated at Seoul St. Mary's Hospital, Republic of Korea,
between June 2015 and August 2017 (Bae 2019 Methods 2.2, Table 1). Mean
age was 63 years (range 21-98) and mean body weight 61.6 kg (range
30.0-126.7); 139 patients were male and 81 female. Mean serum creatinine
was 1.7 mg/dL (range 0.20-13.3) and mean Cockcroft-Gault creatinine
clearance 77.0 mL/min (range 4.57-279; median 72.4 mL/min per the
Discussion). Twenty patients received hemodialysis and nine received
CRRT during vancomycin therapy. The same information is available
programmatically via `readModelDb("Bae_2019_vancomycin")$population`.

# Source trace

| Equation / parameter | Value | Source location |
|---|---|---|
| Two-compartment, first-order elimination, IV infusion | n/a | Results 3.1; Methods 2.3 |
| `CL = theta1 * (CLCR/72)^theta2` (no HD, no CRRT) | n/a | Table 2, row 'CL' |
| `lcl` (theta1) | 2.82 L/h | Table 2 |
| `e_crcl_cl` (theta2) | 0.836 | Table 2 |
| `lcl_crrt` (CL in CRRT patients) | 0.716 L/h | Table 2; Results 3.1 |
| `lcl_dial` (CL in HD patients) | 0.334 L/h | Table 2; Results 3.1 |
| `lvc` (V1) | 31.8 L | Table 2 |
| `lq` (Q) | 11.7 L/h | Table 2 |
| `V2 = theta3 * (WT/60)` | n/a | Table 2, row 'V2' |
| `lvp` (theta3) | 75.4 L | Table 2 |
| `etalcl` (99.2% CV) | 0.685147 | Table 2; CV-to-variance via Methods Eq. 3 |
| `etalvp` (49.2% CV) | 0.216775 | Table 2; CV-to-variance via Methods Eq. 3 |
| `propSd` | 0.253 | Table 2, row 'sigma prop' |
| Log-normal IIV `P = theta * exp(eta)` | n/a | Methods Eq. 1 |

Methods Eq. 3 defines `CV(%) = sqrt(exp(omega^2) - 1) x 100`, so each
variance is `log(1 + CV^2)`.

# Virtual cohort and simulation

This reproduces the simulation design of Bae 2019 Section 3.2 and
Figure 3: 1 g vancomycin every 24 h as a 1-h infusion to 60-kg patients
in four groups. Group 1 has CLCR 100 mL/min, group 2 CLCR 40 mL/min,
group 3 is on CRRT and group 4 on hemodialysis (CLCR is not read in
groups 3 and 4). The paper simulated 1000 subjects per group; 200 are
used here. Figure 3 shows eight doses (0 to 168 h) and a 192-h horizon,
so the same schedule is used.

```{r cohort}
n_sub <- 200L
groups <- tibble(
  group = factor(1:4),
  label = c("1: CLCR 100 mL/min", "2: CLCR 40 mL/min", "3: CRRT", "4: Hemodialysis"),
  CRCL = c(100, 40, 72, 72),
  RRT_CRRT_STATUS = c(0L, 0L, 1L, 0L),
  RRT_HEMODIAL_STATUS = c(0L, 0L, 0L, 1L),
  WT = 60
)

dose_mg <- 1000
dose_times <- seq(0, 168, by = 24)
obs_times <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 192, by = 0.5), dose_times + 1)))

build_group <- function(g) {
  ids <- (as.integer(g$group) - 1L) * n_sub + seq_len(n_sub)
  dose_rows <- tidyr::expand_grid(id = ids, time = dose_times) |>
    mutate(evid = 1L, amt = dose_mg, rate = dose_mg / 1)
  obs_rows <- tidyr::expand_grid(id = ids, time = obs_times) |>
    mutate(evid = 0L, amt = 0, rate = 0)
  bind_rows(dose_rows, obs_rows) |>
    mutate(
      cmt = "central",
      group = g$group,
      CRCL = g$CRCL,
      RRT_CRRT_STATUS = g$RRT_CRRT_STATUS,
      RRT_HEMODIAL_STATUS = g$RRT_HEMODIAL_STATUS,
      WT = g$WT
    )
}

events <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(groups)), function(i) build_group(groups[i, ])) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  arrange(id, time, desc(evid)) |>
  as.data.frame()
```

```{r simulate}
mod <- readModelDb("Bae_2019_vancomycin")
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20190509)
sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = events, keep = "group") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  left_join(groups |> select(group, label), by = "group")

mod_typical <- rxode2::zeroRe(mod)
typ_events <- events |> filter(id %in% ((0:3) * n_sub + 1L))
sim_typical <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_typical, events = typ_events, keep = "group") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  left_join(groups |> select(group, label), by = "group")
```

# Replicate Figure 3

```{r figure3, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 8, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 3 of Bae 2019: median (black) and 90% prediction interval (blue dashed) of vancomycin concentration after 1 g every 24 h as a 1-h infusion. Red lines mark the representative Ctrough (10 mg/L) and Cpeak (50 mg/L) targets."}
fig3 <- sim |>
  group_by(label, time) |>
  summarise(
    med = median(Cc),
    lo = quantile(Cc, 0.05),
    hi = quantile(Cc, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(fig3, aes(time)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = med)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = lo), colour = "blue", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = hi), colour = "blue", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(10, 50), colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~label, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Vancomycin concentration (mg/L)") +
  theme_bw()
```

The four panels reproduce the ordering and shape of Figure 3: exposure
rises from group 1 to group 4, and the hemodialysis group is still
accumulating at 192 h because its clearance (0.334 L/h) gives a terminal
half-life of several days. The medians match the published panels
closely in groups 3 and 4. The published 90% intervals are wider in
those two groups (at 192 h roughly 10-100 mg/L for hemodialysis, against
about 25-80 mg/L here); the paper does not state whether its intervals
include residual error, and the intervals here show between-subject
variability only.

# Typical-value checks

The clearance that each group's typical patient receives follows
directly from Table 2. Both sides use the same parameters, so the bound
is tight.

```{r cl_check}
cl_typ <- sim_typical |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(cl = first(cl), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(cl_table2 = c(2.82 * (100 / 72)^0.836, 2.82 * (40 / 72)^0.836, 0.716, 0.334))
knitr::kable(cl_typ, digits = 3, caption = "Typical clearance (L/h) by simulation group.")
stopifnot(max(abs(cl_typ$cl / cl_typ$cl_table2 - 1)) < 1e-8)
```

# Noncompartmental analysis

## Single-dose identity check

A single 1 g dose to each group's typical patient, followed for long
enough to capture the hemodialysis terminal phase, must give
`AUC(0-inf) = Dose / CL`.

```{r sd_identity}
# Follow each group for roughly 13-15 terminal half-lives: long enough to
# make the AUC extrapolation negligible, short enough that the fast groups
# do not decay into solver round-off.
sd_end <- c(600, 900, 1800, 3000)
sd_events <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(groups)), function(i) {
  g <- groups[i, ]
  sd_times <- sort(unique(c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12,
                            exp(seq(log(16), log(sd_end[i]), length.out = 120)))))
  bind_rows(
    tibble(time = 0, evid = 1L, amt = dose_mg, rate = dose_mg),
    tibble(time = sd_times, evid = 0L, amt = 0, rate = 0)
  ) |>
    mutate(
      id = i, cmt = "central", group = g$group, CRCL = g$CRCL,
      RRT_CRRT_STATUS = g$RRT_CRRT_STATUS,
      RRT_HEMODIAL_STATUS = g$RRT_HEMODIAL_STATUS, WT = g$WT
    )
}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  arrange(id, time, desc(evid)) |>
  as.data.frame()

sd_sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_typical, events = sd_events, keep = "group") |>
  as.data.frame()

sd_conc <- sd_sim |>
  filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  select(id, time, Cc, group, cl)
sd_dose <- sd_events |>
  filter(evid == 1) |>
  select(id, time, amt, group)

sd_nca <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(
  PKNCA::PKNCAconc(sd_conc, Cc ~ time | group + id),
  PKNCA::PKNCAdose(sd_dose, amt ~ time | group + id),
  intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = Inf, aucinf.obs = TRUE, half.life = TRUE)
))

sd_check <- as.data.frame(sd_nca$result) |>
  filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("aucinf.obs", "half.life")) |>
  select(group, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES) |>
  left_join(sd_conc |> distinct(group, cl), by = "group") |>
  mutate(dose_over_cl = dose_mg / cl, pct_diff = 100 * (aucinf.obs / dose_over_cl - 1))

sd_check |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Group" = group,
    "AUC0-inf (mg*h/L)" = aucinf.obs,
    "Terminal t1/2 (h)" = half.life,
    "CL (L/h)" = cl,
    "Dose/CL (mg*h/L)" = dose_over_cl,
    "% diff" = pct_diff
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Single-dose AUC(0-inf) of the typical patient against Dose/CL.")

# Deterministic solve against its own closed form: residual is trapezoid and
# extrapolation error only.
stopifnot(max(abs(sd_check$pct_diff)) < 1)
```

## Day-8 dosing interval against the published simulation

Bae 2019 Results 3.2 reports the simulated median `Cpeak,ss` and
`Ctrough,ss` for groups 1 and 2. The last dosing interval (168-192 h)
is re-based to start at time 0 for PKNCA.

```{r nca_ss}
ss_conc <- sim |>
  filter(!is.na(Cc), time >= 168, time <= 192) |>
  mutate(time = time - 168) |>
  select(id, time, Cc, group)

ss_nca <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(
  PKNCA::PKNCAconc(ss_conc, Cc ~ time | group + id),
  intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = 24, cmax = TRUE, ctrough = TRUE, auclast = TRUE)
))
ss_res <- as.data.frame(ss_nca$result)

simulated <- ss_res |>
  filter(group %in% c("1", "2"), PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "ctrough")) |>
  select(group, PPTESTCD, PPORRES)

# Results 3.2 prints group 2 as 'Cpeak,ss and Ctrough,ss were ... 14 mg/L and
# 40 mg/L, respectively', which is the reverse order of group 1's pair; a peak
# below the trough is impossible and Figure 3 panel 2 shows a peak near 40 and
# a trough near 14, so the pair is read as Cpeak 40, Ctrough 14.
reference <- data.frame(group = c("1", "2"), cmax = c(34, 40), ctrough = c(8, 14))

cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = simulated,
  reference = reference,
  by = "group",
  units = c(cmax = "mg/L", ctrough = "mg/L"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(
  cmp,
  caption = "Median simulated Cpeak and Ctrough over 168-192 h vs Bae 2019 Results 3.2 (groups 1 and 2).",
  align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r")
)
attr(cmp, "footnote")

ss_summary <- ss_res |>
  filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "ctrough", "auclast")) |>
  group_by(group, PPTESTCD) |>
  summarise(median = median(PPORRES), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = median)
ss_summary |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Group" = group,
    "AUC168-192 (mg*h/L)" = auclast,
    "Cmax (mg/L)" = cmax,
    "Ctrough (mg/L)" = ctrough
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Median day-8 exposure by group (all four groups).")

gate <- simulated |>
  group_by(group, PPTESTCD) |>
  summarise(sim = median(PPORRES), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(
    reference |> pivot_longer(-group, names_to = "PPTESTCD", values_to = "pub"),
    by = c("group", "PPTESTCD")
  ) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * (sim / pub - 1))
stopifnot(
  nrow(gate) == 4,
  # Peaks: the 1-h infusion into V1 = 31.8 L sets the peak; a wrong V1, dose
  # or infusion duration moves it by far more than this.
  all(abs(gate$pct[gate$PPTESTCD == "cmax"]) < 15),
  # Troughs: the published values are rounded to whole mg/L and miss in
  # opposite directions in the two groups (see below), so only the order of
  # magnitude is gated here.
  all(abs(gate$pct[gate$PPTESTCD == "ctrough"]) < 30),
  # Group ordering of Figure 3: exposure rises from group 1 to group 4.
  all(diff(ss_summary$auclast) > 0)
)
```

The simulated peaks agree with the published values to within about
10%. The troughs miss in opposite directions, by roughly 10-20%: low in
group 1 (CLCR 100 mL/min) and high in group 2 (CLCR 40 mL/min); the
typical patient's troughs (6.6 and 17.3 mg/L) show the same pattern. The
published pair implies a clearance ratio between the two groups of about
1.65, whereas Table 2 gives `(100/40)^0.836 = 2.15`; no reading of the
printed covariate model reproduces both troughs, and the CRRT and
hemodialysis panels (which do not read CLCR) match Figure 3 closely. The
model is kept exactly as printed in Table 2.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Errata and supplements.** No erratum or correction was found
  (Europe PMC, 2026-11-25), and the article has no supplementary
  material; Table 2 is the sole source of the parameter values.
* **Residual error.** Methods Eq. 2 describes a combined additive plus
  proportional error model, but Table 2 reports only a proportional
  component (0.253). The model uses proportional error only. The value is
  read as a standard deviation (25.3%); a later vancomycin MIPD
  comparison (Oda 2023, Clin Transl Sci) transcribes the same model with
  a 25.3% proportional residual error.
* **IIV.** Table 2 reports IIV on CL and V2 only. The Discussion states
  that the Shiny tool optimizes the post hoc etas 'of CL and V1'; Table 2,
  the estimation table, is followed.
* **CRRT and hemodialysis clearances.** Table 2 and Results 3.1 assign
  0.716 L/h to CRRT and 0.334 L/h to hemodialysis; the Discussion states
  the reverse. Table 2 is followed, and Figure 3 (group 4, hemodialysis,
  has the highest exposure) agrees with it. The CL eta is applied to the
  CRRT and hemodialysis clearances as well as to the CLCR-driven
  clearance, since the paper reports a single IIV on CL.
* **Mutually exclusive RRT indicators.** The paper does not describe a
  patient on both therapies; at most one of `RRT_HEMODIAL_STATUS` and
  `RRT_CRRT_STATUS` should be 1. CLCR is not read when either is 1.
* **Typical CL.** Results 3.1 quotes a typical CL of 2.80 L/h at CLCR
  72 mL/min, while Table 2 gives theta1 = 2.82 L/h; the Table 2 final
  estimate is used (2.80 is the bootstrap median).
* **Simulation design.** Section 3.2 says 'daily 1 g for 7 days' but
  Figure 3 shows eight doses (0 to 168 h); the figure's schedule is used.
  Cohort size is 200 per group rather than 1000.
* **Units.** The Methods outlier cut-off and the Figure 3 y-axis are
  printed in ng/mL, but every value (target trough 10-20, peak target
  50, Cpeak,ss 34) is in mg/L, the unit used here.
